name: Phenylpiracetam (Phenotropil)

lead: Phenylpiracetam is a Soviet-era racetam with a phenyl group added to piracetam. It is prescribed in Russia and sold through gray channels elsewhere.
People take it for energy, drive and reduced fatigue, which supports training and study consistency. Animal work on its S-form reported lower weight gain.

paras: The R-enantiomer inhibits the dopamine transporter and it also binds nicotinic receptors; onset is within an hour and half-life about three to five hours.

Reported effects are insomnia, agitation, flushing and raised blood pressure. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and under 18 in Russian labelling, unapproved in the US and banned in-competition by WADA. Supplement products have been found mislabelled.

angle.text: Users take it for energy and drive on long days and before workouts. Animal studies of its S-form reported lower body weight gain on a Western diet, which some body-composition users cite.[7]

lead: Phenylpiracetam, also called fonturacetam, carphedon or by the brand Phenotropil, is a stimulant-leaning racetam: piracetam with a phenyl group added to the pyrrolidone ring. It was developed in the Soviet Union for cosmonauts and first described in 1983.[1][2] People take it for mental energy, motivation and stamina, which supports training, study and long working days; in animal work the S-enantiomer also reduced weight gain, a result that interests some body-composition users.[3]

It is a prescription drug in Russia, approved there in 2003, for conditions such as cerebrovascular insufficiency, apathy and asthenia.[1][4] In the United States it is an unapproved drug, and it is the only racetam on the WADA prohibited list for in-competition use.[1] The first nootropic prohibited in sport was fonturacetam, in 1998.[5]

Research is mostly Russian clinical work in stroke, epilepsy and neurotic disorders, together with animal studies and reviews of its pharmacology.[6][7][8] In lifting and supplement forums it is discussed as an add-on to pre-workout stacks and for focus, with users commonly mentioning that tolerance builds.[9][10] Surveillance studies of purchased supplements have found racetam-class and other unapproved drugs sold in nootropic products, not always as labelled.[11][12]
infobox: Rx in Russia and Australia; unapproved in US; WADA-prohibited[1]

paras: Chemically, phenylpiracetam is a 4-phenyl analogue of piracetam. Unlike most racetams it contains a phenylethylamine backbone, which is why it is sometimes also classed as a substituted phenethylamine.[1] It is a racemic mixture of two mirror-image forms, the (R) and (S) enantiomers, which differ in their activity: the (R) form is the one that strongly stimulates locomotor activity in animal tests, while the (S) form has been studied separately for effects on body weight.[1][3]
In Russia it is manufactured as a prescription tablet under brands such as Phenotropil and Actitropil, and it is also sold online as a nootropic.[1]

Users describe taking phenylpiracetam for energy, motivation and pre-workout drive, with the idea that more consistent sessions and better focus on long days feed into physique and routine. A 2017 study in mice found that the S-isomer reduced body weight gain on a Western diet without changing locomotor activity, and the authors tested effects on blood glucose and leptin as well.[3] Appetite reduction has been noted with extended use in humans, according to reference summaries.[1]

In Russia it is prescribed for cerebrovascular deficiency, depression, apathy, attention and memory problems, recovery after brain injury, and as an add-on in epilepsy.[1][4] A 2024 Russian review discusses prospects in cerebral ischemia, neurodegenerative disease, epilepsy, asthenia and metabolic syndrome, and lists anxiolytic, antiasthenic, antidepressant, anti-inflammatory and anticonvulsant effects.[6]

Published human studies are largely Russian and appeared in Russian-language journals.[6] A controlled trial of 400 patients with ischemic stroke gave the main group (200 patients) three courses of phenotropil at 400 mg/day during the year after stroke as part of rehabilitation; the authors reported significantly better recovery of neurological function and daily living activities in the treated group, measured on the Barthel, Lindmark, Scandinavian, Merton and Sutton scales.[8]

In 75 patients with symptomatic post-traumatic epilepsy, a randomized comparison of nootropics and antioxidants added to standard therapy reported fewer seizures, better cognitive function and quality of life, and lower depression scores.[13] In a 12-week controlled study of 70 patients with cardiovascular disease and mild neurotic, somatoform or depressive disorders, phenotropil was compared with another drug (Pantogam Active); the authors reported satisfactory tolerability for both, with the anxiolytic effect of phenotropil declining after 4 to 8 weeks.[14]

A 2026 registered phase 1 study lists racetam-class compounds among those used to test IQ-testing reliability in healthy adults.[15] Animal studies report anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects of the R-isomer in mice.[16] No controlled trials have examined it as a physique or training aid in healthy people.

Reported effects include insomnia, agitation, flushing, a feeling of warmth and raised blood pressure; reduced appetite has been noted with extended use.[1] No overdoses have been reported, according to the encyclopedia summary.[1] Labels in Russia list pregnancy, breastfeeding and under-18 age as contraindications.[4]

The (R)-enantiomer is a selective dopamine transporter inhibitor with weaker action at the norepinephrine transporter, and phenylpiracetam also binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in mouse cortex.[1][16][3] Racetams as a class have also been described as modulators of AMPA receptors.[1][7] It was in 2014 that the R-enantiomer, coded MRZ-9547, was identified as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor, which gave a modern explanation for its stimulant-like profile.[1]

Oral bioavailability is reported near complete, onset within an hour and half-life of three to five hours in humans, with little metabolism; roughly 40 percent is reported excreted in urine and the rest in bile and sweat. Human pharmacokinetic data are largely unpublished.[1]

The compound was developed at the Institute of Biomedical Problems of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Moscow, under psychopharmacologist Valentina Akhapkina, as a drug for cosmonauts facing the stresses of spaceflight, and was described in 1983.[1][2] Cosmonaut Aleksandr Serebrov, who spent 197 days on Mir, said it was included in Soyuz emergency medical kits and called it "the equalizer of the whole organism."[1] It was approved for medical use in Russia in 2003.[1] A development program for Parkinson-related fatigue was noted around 2014 but was not reported as advanced.[1]

It is prescription-only in Russia and Australia (Schedule 4), unapproved in the United States, where its use in supplements or foods is described as unlawful, and prohibited by WADA in competition.[1] A 2023 review notes fonturacetam was the first nootropic banned in sport, in 1998.[5]

subs.h: Use in lifting and nootropic communities
paras: On T Nation forums it appears in long-running nootropic threads. One poster described it as a "great add-on to preworkout and for studying" while noting tolerance buildup.[9] Another, asking about nootropics for mind-muscle connection, said they had read it was a good option and was banned from professional competitions.[10] Others describe it as expensive or list it among compounds they intended to try.[17]

Studies of online supplements have found unapproved drugs in nootropic products, sometimes at pharmaceutical-level amounts and not always as labelled; a 2025 surveillance study by 12 official medicines control laboratories in Europe and Australia examined illicit smart drugs and their associated dangers.[11][12]

lore.intro: Phenylpiracetam is discussed in lifting and nootropic forums as a stimulant-like stack component for training and studying, often compared with modafinil or caffeine.[9][17]
